Rh-Catalyzed Carbonylative Cyclization of Propargylic Alcohols with
Aryl Boronic Acids
Wenxiang He, Wei-Feng Zheng, and Hui Qian*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 6279−6283
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: 2(3H)-Furanones are tremendously important not
only because of their wide occurrence in bioactive compounds but
also due to their versatility in organic synthesis. Here, a
straightforward approach to 2(3H)-furanones from readily
available tertiary propargylic alcohols with arylboronic acids in
the presence of CO using rhodium as a catalyst has been
established. The method exhibits a broad substrate scope tolerating useful functional groups with a moderate to high
stereoselectivity.
B
utenolides represent privileged motifs commonly found
in natural products, pharmaceuticals, and bioactive
molecules.
1
Moreover, butenolides also serve as versatile
building blocks in the total synthesis of natural products
2,3
and asymmetric catalysis.
4
Of particular interest, 2(3H)-
furanones have also attracted considerable interest due to
their potential in biological activity (Scheme 1c).
5
Thus, the
development of new synthetic methods for 2(3H)-furanones
is of high interest. On the other hand, propargylic alcohols
are easily available and versatile building blocks in organic
synthesis due to the presence of two functionalities.
6
Recently, our group have developed a series of transition-
metal-catalyzed reactions of propargylic alcohols:
7,8
we
reported that under the catalysis of Rh(III), the C−H
functionalization of arenes with tertiary propargylic alcohols
afforded tetra-substituted allenes (Scheme 1a, eq 1).
7a
In
addition, Rh
3+
/Ag
+
-cocatalyzed reaction of propargylic
alcohols with boronic acids would afford allylic alcohols
(Scheme 1a, eq 2).
7b
However, the Pd/H
+
-cocatalyzed
reaction of propargylic alcohols with boronic acids afforded
tri- or tetra-substituted allenes (Scheme 1a, eq 3).
7c
Furthermore, in the presence of CO and water or MeOH,
with Pd and Bro ̷ nsted acid as cocatalysts, propargylic alcohols
would undergo carboxylation, affording 2,3-allenoic acids
7d,e
or allenoates
7f
(Scheme 1a, eq 4). We envisioned that
trapping the allenylic rhodium intermediate in the presence of
CO and boronic acids would result in the formation of not-
readily available thermosensitive allenones under mild
conditions (Scheme 1b).
9,10
However, 2(3H)-furanones
were obtained unexpectedly. Here we wish to report this
Rh-catalyzed carbonylation of tertiary propargylic alcohols
affording 2(3H)-furanones exclusively with good to excellent
stereoselectivity (Scheme 1b).

Initially, 2-phenyloct-3-yn-2-ol 1a and phenylboronic acid
2b were chosen as the model substrates using THF as the
solvent with a CO balloon to test the hypothesis shown in
Scheme 1b. However, the expected product allenone 3ab was
not detected when [RhCl(COD)]
2
was used as the catalyst.
Interestingly, 1% yield of direct coupling product without CO
incorporation allene 4ab,
7c
3% yield of allylic alcohol E-
5ab,
7b
10% yield of E-4-butyl-5-phenyl-3-(1-
phenylethylidene)furan-2(3H)-one E-6ab, 3% yield of its
stereoisomer Z-6ab, and 54% recovery of 1a were detected
(Table 1, entry 1). Different Rh catalysts were then
examined. The yield of E-6ab slightly decreased when
[RhCl(C

was obtained in 44% yield (Table 1, entry 3). To our delight,
when Rh(acac)(C
2

2
was employed, a 71% yield of E-6ab
was obtained together with 9% of Z-6ab (Table 1, entry 4).
We believe that the improvement is caused by the anion of
the rhodium catalyst, where the enolate anion facilitates the
transmetalation rather than the chloride anion. Among the
screened Rh(II) and Rh(III) catalysts, Rh
2
(OAc)
4
and
[Cp*RhCl
2
]
2
did not yield the 2(3H)-furanone product E-
6ab, with 1a recovered with 98% and 87%, respectively
(Table 1, entries 5 and 6). Solvents were found to be crucial
for this transformation. The yield slightly decreased when
toluene or dioxane was used as the solvent (Table 1, entries
7 and 8), while the efficiency decreased sharply when MeCN
or MeOH was used (Table 1, entries 9 and 10). No
improvement was obtained when DCE was employed (Table
1, entry 11). Among all of the solvents examined, THF was
still the best. Thus, the optimal reaction conditions have been
identified as shown in entry 4 of Table 1.
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we then
explored the substrate scope (Scheme 2). A variety of tertiary
propargylic alcohols with electron-rich, electron-neutral, and
electron-deficient moieties substituted aryl groups (R
1
) could
be tolerated, affording 2(3H)-furanones in moderate to high
yields. The stereoselectivity was established by single-crystal
X-ray analysis of Z-6ba and E-6ga. The steric hindrance has
an obvious influence on the stereoselectivity since the E/Z
selectivity of 6da, 6ca, and 6ba dropped in the order of ortho,
meta, and para-substitution. Various functional groups with
synthetic potentials, such as trimethylsilyl, ester, methoxyl,
halide, cyano, etc., may be smoothly tolerated within the
structure of propargylic alcohols for the reaction with
arylboronic acid 2a in the presence of CO to afford E-6ea,
E-6ga, E-6ha, E-6ia, E-6ja, E-6ka, E-6la, and 6ra in 56−77%
isolated yields. Furthermore, 1-naphthyl was also tolerated
(E-6ma). Apart from R
1
being an aryl group, the methyl
group was also compatible, affording the desired 2(3H)-
furanone 6na in 72% yield. By changing R
2
to a longer alkyl
chain such as ethyl or n-propyl, E-6oa and E-6pa were
obtained in 72% and 67% yields, respectively, with a
stereoselectivity higher than that of E-6aa. R
3
groups may
be alkyl groups such as cyclopropyl, −(CH
2
)
3
CN, and
−(CH
2
)
3
Cl, which worked smoothly to afford the corre-
sponding products (E-6qa, 6ra, and 6sa). Besides, the
reactivity of arylboronic acids was also investigated with 1c,
affording E-6cb, E-6cc, and E-6cd with a moderate
stereoselectivity. We have also tried 3-furanboronic acid and
3-thiopheneboronic acid; however, the yield and stereo-
selectivity were not good (see the Supporting Information for
more details).
A possible catalytic cycle is proposed as shown in Scheme
3.
11,12
An arylrhodium intermediate B formed by the
transmetalation of Rh(I) species A with arylboronic acids
would undergo CO insertion to form the acyl rhodium
intermediate C. The OH-directed syn-insertion would result
in the formation of alkenylrhodium intermediate D.
7a,b
The
second CO insertion of the intermediate D, followed by an
endomode insertion with the carbonyl group, would form
intermediate F. We also conducted the experiment with
13
CO
to confirm the double CO insertion process (see the
Supporting Information for more details). Subsequent 1,3-
allylic Rh migration would form intermediate G with the OH
group at the β-position of the rhodium atom. Subsequently,
β-OH elimination would then deliver the targeted products
and regenerate the catalytically active Rh(I) species to finish
the catalytic cycle. Another potential mechanism could
involve the addition of arylcarbonyl to the Rh-carbonyl to
form F′, followed by rearrangement of the carbon−rhodium

bond to yield a furan featuring a rhodium alkoxide G′, which
was the enolate form of intermediate G.
In conclusion, we have developed the Rh-catalyzed
carbonylative cyclization of tertiary propargylic alcohols
with arylboronic acids in the presence of CO affording
2(3H)-furanones. The reaction proceeds via double CO
insertion, and the mild reaction conditions enable a wide
substrate scope tolerating many functional groups with a high
stereoselectivity for the exo-C�C bond. Further studies
related to this area are being pursued in our laboratory.
